stimulus.text:
Painting: William B. T. Trego's The March to Valley Forge, December 19, 1777 (painted 1883) shows George Washington on a white horse leading a column of Continental soldiers through snow. The men march in ragged clothes, some barefoot, carrying muskets and a drum, while officers on horseback ride beside them.

Letter: “I am now convinced beyond a doubt, that unless some great and capital change suddenly takes place in that line this Army must inevitably be reduced to one or other of these three things. Starve—dissolve—or disperse, in order to obtain subsistence in the best manner they can.”
—George Washington to Henry Laurens, president of Congress, Valley Forge, December 23, 1777
stimulus.source_note: William B. T. Trego, The March to Valley Forge, December 19, 1777 (1883); George Washington to Henry Laurens, December 23, 1777. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: The army that marched out of Valley Forge in June 1778 differed from the army that marched in mainly because

options.text: Congress had voted to end the war and seek peace
options.misconception: Congress did not vote to end the war in 1778; the war went on for five more years, until 1783.

options.text: The British had withdrawn all their troops from America
options.misconception: British troops stayed in America until 1783, holding New York City and other posts after Valley Forge.

options.text: Baron von Steuben had drilled it into a disciplined professional force
France had sent a fleet to blockade the Delaware River
options.misconception: The French fleet did not arrive in American waters until the summer of 1778, after the army left Valley Forge.

rationales.C: Steuben's drill at Valley Forge turned raw Continentals into soldiers who could stand in line against British regulars, as they showed at Monmouth.
rationales.D: The French fleet reached American waters in the summer of 1778, after the army had already left Valley Forge.
rationales.A: Congress did not seek peace in 1778; the war continued until the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
rationales.B: British troops remained in America for five more years, holding New York until the war's end.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the two marches. Ragged men walked into Valley Forge in December; a drilled army walked out in June.
2. Ask what changed between them. Steuben, a Prussian officer, trained the men through the winter in drill and discipline.
3. Check the proof. At Monmouth days later, the Continentals stood and fought the British in the open, which they could not have done before.
Remember: training is a cause, not a decoration — ask what the army could do after it that it could not do before. Background: the Battle of Monmouth was fought in June 1778, days after the army left Valley Forge.
